title: Control Systems
description: Control Systems develops the analysis and design of feedback systems that remain stable, accurate, responsive, and robust in the presence of disturbances, noise, uncertainty, delays, and actuator limits. Students progress from multi-domain modeling and classical frequency-domain design to state-space control, estimation, digital implementation, robustness, optimization, nonlinear behavior, and experimental validation. One rigorous common core serves all three degrees. Electrical Engineering emphasizes circuits, motors, power, sensing, and embedded implementation, Mechanical Engineering emphasizes physical modeling, actuators, mechatronics, and experiments, and graduate students add proof, MIMO analysis, estimation, optimization, uncertainty, and research-quality design evidence.

resources.title: Control Tutorials for MATLAB and Simulink

resources.title: Python Control Systems Library
resources.description: Open analysis and design environment for transfer functions, state space, frequency response, synthesis, and simulation.

resources.title: MATLAB Control System Toolbox
resources.description: Industry-standard modeling, analysis, tuning, estimation, and control-design workflows.

resources.title: IEEE Control Systems Society
resources.description: Research, standards, conferences, technical communities, and current directions in control.

resources.title: Brian Douglas
resources.description: Exceptionally clear visual explanations of transfer functions, stability, root locus, Bode/Nyquist, PID, and state space.

resources.title: Steve Brunton
resources.description: Dynamic systems, state-space control, estimation, system identification, nonlinear methods, and data-driven modeling.

resources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare
resources.description: University lectures and demonstrations spanning mechanical, electrical, aerospace, and graduate control.

resources.title: MATLAB
resources.description: Practical Simulink, PID tuning, control design, system identification, and deployment workflows.

topics.title: Course Orientation, Feedback Concepts, and Control Objectives
topics.description: This opening unit explains why feedback is powerful: it can make systems accurate, stable, robust, and responsive despite disturbances and uncertainty. Students learn the vocabulary used throughout the course.

children.title: Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control
children.description: Students learn the difference between commanding a system blindly and using measured output to correct behavior.

children.title: Control Objectives and Tradeoffs
children.description: Control design is a negotiation among speed, stability, accuracy, robustness, effort, and noise sensitivity.

children.title: Rise time, settling time, overshoot, steady-state error
Actuator limits, sensor noise, and design compromises
Control System Examples
children.description: Examples make abstract diagrams concrete by showing control in electrical, mechanical, thermal, process, aerospace, and robotic systems.

children.title: Cruise control, motor speed, temperature, liquid level
Aircraft autopilot and spacecraft attitude control

topics.title: Dynamic System Modeling Across Domains
topics.description: Controls begins with models. This unit teaches students to represent physical systems with equations that capture how inputs, states, and outputs evolve over time.

children.title: Mechanical, Electrical, Thermal, and Fluid Analogies
children.description: Students learn common modeling patterns that transfer across engineering domains.

children.title: Input, Output, State, and Disturbance Variables
children.description: Clear variable definitions keep models connected to measurable and controllable quantities.

children.title: Model Validation and Limits
children.description: A useful model is not necessarily complete. Students learn how to judge what is included and what is ignored.

children.title: Experimental data and parameter estimation overview

topics.title: Laplace Transforms, Transfer Functions, and Linearization
topics.description: This unit converts differential-equation models into algebraic input-output relationships. Transfer functions become the language for classical control analysis and design.

children.title: Laplace Transform Review
children.description: Students review the transform tools needed to solve linear dynamic systems and interpret poles and zeros.

children.title: Transfer Functions
children.description: Transfer functions summarize how a linear time-invariant system maps inputs to outputs.

children.title: Input-output ratio with zero initial conditions
Poles, zeros, gain, and system order
Proper and strictly proper transfer functions
Linearization Around Operating Points
children.description: Many real systems are nonlinear, so students learn how local linear models support classical control.

children.title: Small-signal models and limits of validity

topics.title: Block Diagrams, Signal Flow Graphs, and Feedback Architecture
topics.description: Control systems are often easier to reason about as interconnected blocks. This unit teaches how to reduce diagrams and identify the functional roles inside a loop.

children.title: Block Diagram Algebra
children.description: Students learn to simplify series, parallel, and feedback interconnections into equivalent transfer functions.

children.title: Signal Flow Graphs
children.description: Signal flow graphs provide a systematic alternative for complex interconnections.

children.title: Feedback Architecture
children.description: Students learn how controllers, plants, sensors, actuators, references, and disturbances fit together.

children.title: Plant, controller, sensor, actuator, and comparator

topics.title: Time-Domain Response and Performance Specifications
topics.description: This unit connects transfer functions to observable behavior over time. Students learn how system poles shape transients, steady-state response, and design specifications.

children.title: First- and Second-Order System Response
children.description: Students learn canonical response shapes that appear repeatedly in engineering control systems.

children.title: Performance Measures
children.description: Design specifications turn a desired behavior into measurable targets.

children.title: Rise time, peak time, percent overshoot
Steady-State Error and System Type
children.description: Students learn how loop structure determines tracking accuracy for common inputs.

children.title: Position, velocity, and acceleration error constants
Tracking step, ramp, and parabolic references

topics.title: Stability Analysis and Routh-Hurwitz Criterion
topics.description: Stability is the first requirement of useful feedback. This unit teaches students how to determine whether closed-loop poles produce bounded, reliable behavior.

children.title: Pole Locations and Stability
children.description: Students connect pole position to whether a continuous-time system decays, oscillates, or grows.

children.title: Left-half plane, right-half plane, and imaginary-axis poles
Routh-Hurwitz Criterion
children.description: Routh-Hurwitz tests stability without explicitly solving high-order characteristic equations.

children.title: Special cases: zero first-column entry and row of zeros
Stability Under Parameter Variation
children.description: Students learn how gain and parameter changes can move a system from stable to unstable.

topics.title: Root Locus Analysis and Design
topics.description: Root locus shows how closed-loop poles move as gain changes. This unit turns stability and transient-response ideas into a graphical design method.

children.title: Root Locus Construction Rules
children.description: Students learn the rules that sketch possible closed-loop pole locations without brute-force computation.

children.title: Gain Selection from Root Locus
children.description: Students use the locus to choose gains that meet damping, settling-time, and stability requirements.

children.title: Root Locus Design Thinking
children.description: Root locus becomes a design tool when students see how adding poles and zeros reshapes possible behavior.

children.title: Effect of controller poles and zeros
Tradeoffs among speed, overshoot, and robustness

topics.title: Frequency Response, Bode Plots, and Nyquist Methods
topics.description: Frequency-domain methods reveal robustness, bandwidth, resonance, and stability margins. This unit gives students the core tools used in practical control design.

children.title: Bode Plot Construction and Interpretation
children.description: Students learn how magnitude and phase versus frequency show system behavior across time scales.

children.title: Stability Margins
children.description: Gain and phase margins quantify how much uncertainty a feedback loop can tolerate before instability.

children.title: Nyquist Criterion
children.description: Nyquist analysis generalizes stability assessment using open-loop frequency response.

children.title: Relationship to Bode and closed-loop stability

topics.title: PID Control and Controller Tuning
topics.description: PID control is the most common practical controller family. This unit teaches what proportional, integral, and derivative actions do and how to tune them responsibly.

children.title: PID Terms and Their Effects
children.description: Students learn how each PID term changes speed, error, damping, and noise sensitivity.

children.title: Integral action and zero steady-state error
Derivative action, damping, and noise amplification
Tuning Methods
children.description: Tuning links desired behavior to controller parameters through rules, models, or iteration.

children.title: Practical PID Issues
children.description: Real PID loops must handle saturation, windup, derivative filtering, and sample time.

topics.title: Lead, Lag, and Loop-Shaping Compensation
topics.description: This unit teaches students how to shape loop behavior beyond PID. Lead, lag, and loop-shaping methods connect root locus and frequency response design.

children.title: Lead Compensation
children.description: Lead compensation adds phase and improves transient response and stability margins.

children.title: Lag Compensation
children.description: Lag compensation improves steady-state accuracy while trying to preserve acceptable transient behavior.

children.title: Impact on bandwidth and response speed
Loop-Shaping Workflow
children.description: Students learn a practical frequency-domain workflow for meeting tracking, disturbance, and robustness goals.

children.title: Shape low-, mid-, and high-frequency behavior
Check sensitivity, noise, and actuator effort

topics.title: State-Space Modeling, Controllability, and Observability
topics.description: State-space methods support multi-input, multi-output systems and modern control design. This unit introduces dynamic models in terms of states, inputs, outputs, and matrices.

children.title: State-Space Representation
children.description: Students learn to rewrite dynamic systems as first-order vector equations.

children.title: State, input, output, and feedthrough matrices
Realizations from physical models and transfer functions
Controllability
children.description: Controllability asks whether inputs can move the system state where it needs to go.

children.title: Observability
children.description: Observability asks whether available measurements contain enough information to infer internal state.

topics.title: State Feedback, Observers, and Estimation Overview
topics.description: This unit shows how state-space models become controllers and estimators. Students learn the ideas behind pole placement, observers, and modern estimation without overloading the first course.

children.title: State Feedback and Pole Placement
children.description: Students learn how full-state feedback can assign closed-loop dynamics when a system is controllable.

children.title: Observers
children.description: Observers estimate states that cannot be measured directly, enabling state feedback in realistic systems.

children.title: Estimation and Kalman Filter Preview
children.description: Students get a conceptual bridge to stochastic estimation and sensor fusion.

children.title: Kalman filter applications in robotics, navigation, and embedded control

topics.title: Digital Control and Sampled-Data Implementation
topics.description: Most modern controllers run in software. This unit introduces sampling, discrete-time models, and implementation effects that matter when theory becomes code.

children.title: Sampling and Discretization
children.description: Students learn how continuous signals and controllers become sampled data systems.

children.title: Discrete-Time Transfer Functions and State Space
children.description: Discrete models let students analyze digital controllers with z-domain tools.

children.title: Embedded Implementation Constraints
children.description: Students learn why real-time code, computation delay, quantization, and saturation affect control performance.

topics.title: Robustness, Practical Implementation, and Integrated Applications
topics.description: The final unit pulls the course together around real design concerns: uncertainty, testing, validation, safety, and application-specific constraints.

children.title: Robustness and Uncertainty
children.description: Students learn that models are imperfect and controllers must tolerate parameter variation, disturbances, and unmodeled dynamics.

children.title: Testing, Tuning, and Validation
children.description: A controller is not finished until it is tested against requirements and operating conditions.

children.title: Step tests, frequency tests, and data logging
Integrated Control Applications
children.description: Capstone-style applications help students connect methods to engineering systems.

children.title: Motor control, robotics, power electronics, process control
Safety, fault detection, and fail-safe behavior

topics.title: Optimal Control, LQR, and Model Predictive Control
topics.description: This unit introduces optimization as a systematic way to balance tracking, regulation, actuator effort, and constraints. It gives graduate students a launch point for advanced optimal control while giving undergraduates the design intuition behind widely used modern methods.

children.title: Quadratic performance and LQR
children.description: Students learn how a quadratic objective converts design priorities into an optimal state-feedback law for a linear model.

children.title: Tracking, integral action, and reference management
children.description: Optimal regulation must be extended carefully when the goal is to follow commands without offset.

children.title: Constraints and model predictive control
children.description: Students learn why receding-horizon optimization is valuable when inputs, states, outputs, and rates have hard limits.

children.title: Recursive feasibility and terminal ingredients overview
Optimal-design evaluation
children.description: Students compare optimization-based controllers with classical and pole-placement designs using consistent evidence.

topics.title: Nonlinear Control, System Identification, and Data-Driven Methods
topics.description: The final advanced unit shows where linear models come from, when they fail, and how data can improve them. The goal is disciplined awareness: students should know what these methods claim, what evidence they require, and when a specialized follow-on course is needed.

children.title: Nonlinear dynamics and phase-plane reasoning
children.description: Students learn how equilibria, local linearization, trajectories, and invariant behavior reveal phenomena that a single transfer function cannot capture.

children.title: Lyapunov stability and nonlinear control overview
children.description: Lyapunov functions provide an energy-like way to reason about stability without explicitly solving nonlinear differential equations.

children.title: System identification and experiment design
children.description: Students learn to estimate models from input-output data while separating excitation, fitting, and independent validation.

children.title: Step, impulse, chirp, and multisine experiments
Data-driven and learning-enabled control
children.description: Students examine how modern methods use data while preserving stability, safety, and physical judgment.

children.title: Safe exploration, distribution shift, and verification
